tasks.short: Design and update the customer interface of the online storefront.

steps.what: Define customer needs, commercial priorities and interface constraints.
Arrange storefront templates, navigation and product components in the {ECOMMERCE}.
Implement custom storefront behavior in the {ECOMMERCE} development environment.
Check mobile journeys, accessibility, checkout and consent behavior in the {ECOMMERCE} preview.
Approve and publish the storefront release through the {ECOMMERCE}.
Review conversion and checkout failures in the {BI}.

tasks.design: Configure reusable storefront components and preview templates in the {ECOMMERCE}; use a deterministic generator only for repeated custom patterns. Automated journey checks record results in the {PROJECT}, a merchant approves publication, and the {BI} shows release outcomes.
tasks.previous_blocker: Theme constraints, bespoke changes and manual journey checks made small releases expensive. Existing template features were often used inconsistently.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing theme configuration covers standard layouts. AI-assisted coding reduces the effort of building reusable components and browser checks; no runtime model is required.
tasks.still_hard: Distinctive design, unusual checkout extensions and meaningful accessibility testing still need expertise. Low traffic can make experiment results inconclusive.
tasks.human_edge: Understand customer hesitation and choose which commercial trade-offs deserve a visible interface change.

ambition.what: Weekly selection of a mobile shopping journey improvement

tasks.altitude: The merchant spends less time rebuilding layouts and repeating checks, and more time observing customers. Within an agreed release scope, they can choose and publish small interface improvements.

reach.task: Evaluate mobile navigation and checkout usability
reach.learn: Task-based usability testing, accessible interaction patterns and interpretation of experiment results

evidence.claim: Reusable storefront configuration and deterministic journey checks can reduce repeated implementation work.
Automated accessibility checks cover only part of interface accessibility; human journey testing remains necessary.

assumptions: The merchant controls an existing storefront rather than commissioning an entirely new commerce platform.
Custom development mainly repeats known component patterns; novel interactions remain developer work.
The estimate covers reusable configuration and checks, not a complete redesign.
GDPR and EU AI Act applicability are assessed for the actual implementation. Customer analytics require appropriate consent and data minimisation; national rules govern any employee consultation.
unknowns: Available theme configuration, preview environments and publication permissions
Extent of custom checkout behavior
Existing analytics consent arrangements and event quality
Merchant release authority and required accessibility standard
Whether national rules require employee consultation for the proposed changes
research_questions: Which repeated changes can existing components already handle?
Which shopping journeys cause the most customer difficulty?
Which automated checks predict actual release defects?
new_work: Review generated components and failed journey checks.
Maintain test accounts, fixtures and component templates.
Investigate changes in conversion before attributing them to a release.
Keep rollback instructions and accessibility checks current.

tasks.short: Select and purchase technical services supporting the online storefront.

steps.what: Document service needs, expected volumes, budget and technical constraints.
Request supplier proposals and clarify service coverage through {EMAIL}.
Compare fees, commitments and service levels in a {SPREADSHEET}.

loop.input: Supplier proposals and a fixed service comparison schema
loop.output: Source-linked fee, commitment and service-level fields; unresolved fields marked missing
loop.check: Validate field types and source passages; calculate scenario costs deterministically; review material terms.
loop.stop: One extraction and one repair pass per proposal; unresolved or contradictory terms go to the merchant.
loop.why_not_simpler: Proposals express fees and exclusions in varied prose. Structured supplier submissions should bypass the model.

steps.what: Assess integration, security, data processing and exit terms in the {DOCS}.
Discuss trade-offs and select a supplier with the budget holder.
Approve the purchase and place the service order through the {PROCUREMENT}.

tasks.design: Use a requirements form and supplier request templates in the {PROCUREMENT}, with a bounded extraction loop producing a source-linked comparison in the {DOCS}. Deterministic calculations compare volume scenarios, reviewers assess material risks, and the {PROCUREMENT} places the approved order and updates the service inventory.
tasks.previous_blocker: Proposals used inconsistent terms, while technical and commercial reviews crossed teams. Low purchase frequency rarely justified a custom application.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing purchasing workflows handle requests and approvals. Small extraction routines can now be built cheaply around a stable comparison template.
tasks.still_hard: Integration quality, supplier reliability, negotiation and exit costs require investigation. Missing contractual commitments cannot be inferred from marketing material.
tasks.human_edge: Judge the cost of service failure and negotiate commitments appropriate to the storefront.
tasks.altitude: The merchant prepares comparisons faster and spends more of the purchase cycle testing assumptions with technical reviewers. Purchasing and contract approval rights do not change.

reach.task: Assess technical service costs within the channel budget
reach.learn: Volume-based cost modelling, service dependencies and supplier exit planning

evidence.claim: Structured comparisons, deterministic cost calculations and configured purchasing approvals can support technical service selection.
Extracting proposal terms requires source checks and does not establish supplier suitability or contractual adequacy.

assumptions: This task concerns legitimate hosting, commerce, payment and security services.
The company has a purchasing process that can be configured rather than replaced.
The comparison template is reusable across merchants or purchases; a one-off purchase may justify manual comparison.
GDPR obligations apply to supplier data processing. EU AI Act applicability and any consultation required by national rules depend on the selected service and its use.
unknowns: Existing supplier agreements and renewal dates
Transaction volumes, service dependencies and acceptable outage exposure
Available purchasing workflows and supplier interfaces
Required technical, legal and budget approvals
Applicable employee consultation requirements under national rules
research_questions: Can suppliers submit structured fees and commitments directly?
Which volume and failure scenarios change the supplier ranking?
Can the comparison and extraction template be reused enough to justify upkeep?
new_work: Verify extracted fees, exclusions and renewal terms.
Maintain cost scenarios and purchasing templates.
Record renewal dates, service ownership and exit commitments.

tasks.short: Deliver purchased digital media and resolve customer access failures.

steps.what: Map approved digital assets and licence settings to products in the {ECOMMERCE}.
Validate payment status and delivery eligibility in the {ECOMMERCE}.
Create a download entitlement or licence key in the {ECOMMERCE}.
Send the customer access instructions through {EMAIL}.
Inspect delivery failures and match them to customer orders in the {ECOMMERCE}.
Investigate access complaints and reissue approved entitlements through the {ECOMMERCE}.

tasks.design: Configure native digital fulfilment in the {ECOMMERCE}, including payment checks, entitlement rules and templated notices through {EMAIL}. Use bounded retries and duplicate protection, route unresolved failures to the {HELPDESK}, and require a support specialist to approve exceptional entitlement changes.
tasks.previous_blocker: Routine delivery was often already automated. The remaining friction came from inconsistent asset mappings, weak failure visibility and support staff switching between order and ticket records.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing delivery settings and event-driven workflows can cover much of the gap. Small deterministic integrations are cheaper to build when native ticket routing is insufficient.
tasks.still_hard: Licence disputes, ownership verification and assets already downloaded cannot be resolved through retries. Some third-party licence services have limited interfaces.
tasks.human_edge: Resolve ambiguous access rights and explain a fair remedy when a customer cannot use a legitimate purchase.

ambition.what: Customer self-service recovery of an existing paid download entitlement

tasks.altitude: Routine transfers remain automated, while the merchant checks a smaller exception queue. Support specialists can approve reissues within existing policy; commercial refund rights do not change.

reach.task: Write digital download and licence recovery instructions
reach.learn: Explain access prerequisites, test recovery journeys and distinguish technical failure from disputed entitlement

evidence.claim: Payment-triggered digital delivery, expiring access links and templated notices are established commerce capabilities.
Deterministic retry limits and duplicate protection can reduce delivery handling without a model loop.

assumptions: The company sells digital assets it is entitled to distribute.
Routine payment checks and delivery are already automated; their zero remaining human time is not a new saving.
Shares are illustrative workflow allocations, including system steps, rather than measured employee time savings.
Native settings are used first; the integration range allows a small connector where needed.
GDPR applies to order and access data. Applicable digital-content consumer rules, including delivery and withdrawal conditions, must be reflected in configuration.
EU AI Act obligations depend on any additional AI use; this design needs no model. National rules determine whether employee consultation applies.
unknowns: Current digital delivery, retry and entitlement capabilities
Asset sizes, licence restrictions and external licence-service interfaces
Actual failure volume and support handling time
Customer identity checks and reissue permissions
Current digital-content consent records and retention periods
Whether national rules require consultation for changed support workflows
research_questions: Which failures can native delivery settings already recover?
Can customers recover an existing entitlement without creating a new licence?
What prevents duplicate delivery when payment events are replayed?
new_work: Review unresolved delivery failures and disputed entitlements.
Test new asset mappings before release.
Monitor retry exhaustion, duplicate events and expired links.
Maintain recovery instructions and access permissions.

tasks.short: Develop, check, select and register a domain name for the online business.

steps.what: Define naming goals, target markets and ownership requirements in the {DOCS}.
Develop and refine candidate names in the {DOCS}.

loop.input: Domain brief, approved brand vocabulary and naming exclusions
loop.output: A short candidate list with naming rationale and flagged linguistic uncertainties
loop.check: Check syntax and exclusions deterministically; a person reviews meaning, pronunciation and brand fit.
loop.stop: At most two rounds and twelve candidates; return the shortlist or continue human naming.
loop.why_not_simpler: Useful naming variations depend on language and meaning. A fixed vocabulary combiner cannot assess those relationships.

steps.what: Check availability and renewal prices in a domain registrar {OTHER}.
Check conflicts using trademark and business-name registers {OTHER}.
Select the preferred domain with the merchant and relevant brand stakeholders.
Approve registration and purchase the domain through the domain registrar {OTHER}.

tasks.design: Keep a naming brief and bounded candidate generator in the {DOCS}, then use the domain registrar {OTHER} for native availability and pricing checks. Record legal review and selection in the {WORKFLOW}; require approval before registration and retain ownership and renewal records in the {DOCS}.
tasks.previous_blocker: Naming depended on taste and brand context, while availability and legal checks were separate. Infrequent registrations did not justify custom purchasing software.
tasks.enabler_now: A small language-based drafting loop can widen the initial candidate list. Native registrar settings and an existing approval workflow handle the remaining administration.
tasks.still_hard: Availability changes quickly and does not establish trademark safety. Cross-language meanings, contested names and premium-domain negotiations remain specialist work.
tasks.human_edge: Choose a name customers can trust and judge whether its commercial meaning justifies legal and acquisition risk.
tasks.altitude: Occasional naming projects require less list preparation and registration paperwork. The merchant gains no new brand, legal or purchasing decision rights.

reach.task: Assess a proposed name for reputational and language risks
reach.learn: Audience interpretation, pronunciation testing and coordination of legal and brand review

evidence.claim: Native registrar tools support availability checks, registration and renewal settings; these checks do not establish trademark clearance.
Bounded language-based drafting can suggest name candidates, while meaning and legal suitability require human review.

assumptions: The purchase concerns an available standard-price domain, not a negotiated acquisition.
An existing document and approval environment is available; no dedicated domain application is built.
The estimate excludes legal clearance turnaround and subsequent technical domain configuration.

GDPR applies to registration contact data and any external processing of confidential briefs. EU AI Act obligations depend on the chosen drafting setup; national rules determine any employee consultation.
unknowns: Target countries, languages and required domain extensions
Trademark coverage and internal legal review capacity
Registrar account ownership, access controls and renewal arrangements
Approval thresholds and permitted registration contacts
Whether national rules require consultation for the proposed tooling
research_questions: Can existing registrar features handle all availability and renewal administration?
Which naming constraints eliminate unsuitable candidates before legal review?
Does the low registration frequency justify anything beyond a saved template?
new_work: Review generated candidates for meaning and unsupported implications.
Recheck availability and price immediately before purchase.
Verify organisational ownership and recovery contacts.
Maintain renewal reminders and remove obsolete domain records.

role.altitude: The online merchant spends less time assembling storefront changes, comparing proposal terms and chasing failed downloads. More time goes to customer journeys and commercial trade-offs, with limited release and recovery authority inside agreed policies.
reach: Web and digital interface designer: evaluate shopping journeys and accessible interactions.
Marketing manager: assess service economics and channel dependencies.
Technical writer: improve digital access and recovery instructions.
Public relations specialist: assess naming and reputation risks.
skills_to_grow: Storefront component configuration and release testing
Customer research and cautious interpretation of conversion data
Supplier cost modelling and source verification
Digital entitlement controls and exception handling
role.ambitious_version: A merchant who can run a steady programme of evidence-based storefront improvements and offer reliable customer self-service recovery, while bringing clear technical and commercial evidence to purchasing decisions.
